lesson_title: Nobody Leaves Their Seat: Transverse Waves and Their Quantities
hook_text: A wave sweeps the whole stadium — and not one person moves sideways. So what actually went around?
clip_script: Friday night game, stands packed to the top row. One block leaps up, arms high, drops back down. The next block copies, then the next — and a wave sweeps clean around the ground. Now slow the replay. Nobody changed seats. Every single supporter went straight up and straight down into the same chair. But the wave travelled sideways, right around the stadium. People vertical, wave horizontal — at right angles. That is exactly what transverse means, and it is what a rope does when you flick it. And here is the deep part: what travelled around the ground was not people. It was the energy of standing up, handed from block to block. Every wave in physics runs this same scam — it delivers energy across a distance without delivering any material. Your shout crosses the field without one puff of air making the trip. Four labels measure it: amplitude for the height, wavelength for the spacing, period for the timing, frequency for the count. And one multiplication ties them together: humps per second times length of each hump equals speed. v equals f lambda.
visual_style: Stylised stadium bowl with blocks of supporters lighting up in sequence as the wave circles; freeze-frame on one glowing supporter moving only vertically; energy shown as a bright baton passing block to block; labels and v = f-lambda stamp in at the end.
mood: A crowd celebration that turns into a physics reveal.
pacing: Fast build as the wave circles, hard freeze on the replay moment, slow zoom on the vertical-only movement, brisk labelled recap.
